deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. It is a continuous piece of speculative natural philosophy that belongs with the 'Erdseele' (earth-soul) fragments, which take up Fechner's Zend-Avesta. It continues the argument of the previous page, which proposed that the seat of a planetary mental process lies in the hot, fluid matter just beneath the solidified crust. The argument runs as follows.

(A) Support for the first hypothesis. The relative position of the parts of matter can be governed by internal processes the more, the less it is governed by external motions. This independence from external causes of motion is realised just below the Earth's surface, going inward, to a degree that organic arrangements at the surface could hardly achieve. Riemann's principle, stated as a monotone relation: internal determinability of configuration rises as external mechanical forcing falls. This is a qualitative claim only.

(B) Apparent objections. Some of the facts listed earlier under nos. 4 and 5 (on preceding sheets) seem to contradict the assumption. The chief one, from the previous page, is that only the four 'organic elements' C, H, N, O carry life on the Earth's surface. They would contradict it if the conditions of life observed at the surface were absolutely valid. Riemann argues that they are only relatively valid, for the present surface of the Earth. His reasons:
1. If they were absolute, all of nature except the Earth's surface would be dead. On every other celestial body the temperatures and pressures are such that organic compounds cannot persist.
2. It is absurd to suppose that the organic arose out of the inorganic on the newly cooled crust. To explain even the lowest organisms one must already presuppose an organising principle, that is, a life-process under conditions in which organic compounds could not exist.
Conclusion: the surface conditions hold only for present terrestrial circumstances. The margin states the task as seeing how a life-process is possible under other conditions.

(C) Why exactly C, H, N, O? The reason must lie in properties that set these four elements apart from all others.
1. O, N and H cannot be condensed at all, and these elements are the hardest bodies to condense. The marginal correction says it is their compounds that are hardest to condense, which takes care of the case of solid carbon.
2. Their compounds are very varied and easily decomposed. Riemann notes that this property could be either a consequence of their use in life-processes or the reason for it.

The next page develops property 1 into a physical hypothesis about condensation. In it, liquids are solid particles floating in their own vapour, and each particle can survive only above a minimum pressure that rises with temperature. That hypothesis is meant to explain why the hardest-to-condense elements suit the life-process best.

Nothing on the page is a derivation. Any 'implicit steps' would be purely argumentative, and I have added none.
errors: Carbon is not a gas, and the claim that it 'cannot be condensed at all' is wrong as first written. Riemann's own marginal revision shifts the claim to compounds (CO, CH4) that are hardest to condense, which fixes this.

The claim that O2, N2 and H2 'cannot be condensed at all' was standard before Andrews (1869, critical temperature) and before Cailletet and Pictet (1877, liquefaction of O2 and N2). It is false in modern terms. For the 1850s it was a fair statement of the 'permanent gases' doctrine and not a slip.
The claim that every other celestial body has temperatures and pressures excluding organic compounds is an unsupported sweeping generalisation, even by the knowledge of the time.
Argument 2 rejects abiogenesis by asserting that an 'organising principle' is required. This is a metaphysical premise, not something demonstrated.

results.what: Principle that internal processes govern the configuration of matter in inverse relation to external mechanical disturbance; placement of a planetary 'soul-process' in the fluid layer beneath the crust
Conditions for life on Earth are only relatively valid; life is possible under other temperatures and pressures; life cannot have arisen on the cooled crust from inorganic matter
results.modern_name: Anti-abiogenesis vitalism / cosmic plurality of life
results.usually_credited_to: General 19th-century debate (Liebig, Fechner, H. E. Richter, later Helmholtz and Thomson on cosmozoa)

results.what: Explaining the special role of C, H, N, O by the very low condensability of these elements and their compounds ('permanent gases') and by the variety and easy decomposition of their compounds
results.modern_name: Permanent gases (Faraday 1845); chemical basis of biochemistry

deep.surprise_reason: This is philosophical and chemical speculation of a known kind. Riemann's Fechner-inspired natural-philosophy fragments, including the Erdseele theme, are known from the Werke ('Fragmente philosophischen Inhalts'). The page holds no mathematics and no result anticipating later science. Its wording and its argument structure (the objections and the four organic elements) may be an unpublished detail, but it is minor.

checkable.asserts: The critical temperatures (in K) of O2, N2 and H2 lie below 0 °C. So pressure alone at ordinary temperatures cannot liquefy them, which is why Riemann's contemporaries counted them as 'permanent gases'.

CO and CH4, the carbon compounds Faraday also failed to liquefy, likewise have critical temperatures below 0 °C. This is consistent with Riemann's marginal correction about hard-to-condense compounds.

transcription_corrections: Line 3: 'desto stets[?] von [...] Vorgängen' should probably read 'desto mehr von inneren Vorgängen im Innern der Materie bestimmt werden kann', given the correlative 'desto ... je weniger'.
Line 6: the inserted words read roughly 'unter der Oberfläche der Erde nach Innen zu', not 'die Oberfläche'. The sense is 'below the surface, going inward'.
Lines 7-8: 'mit Ausnahme[?] der Erdrinde irgend erwarten liesse' is doubtful. The sense requires 'in a degree such as could hardly be expected from organic arrangements at the Earth's surface'.
'Unter den folgenden [...] Hypothesen' is more likely 'Thatsachen', since items 4 and 5 are facts that 'contradict our assumption'.
Marginal note beside 'Unter den folgenden...': it reads approximately 'welche wir im Folgenden anfangs betrachten', and the transcription omits it.
'Gegen Ersteres aber spricht folgender Grund' is probably plural ('sprechen folgende Gründe'), since two reasons follow.
'auf der [?] erkalteten Erdrinde' probably reads 'auf der erst erkalteten Erdrinde'.
